summary:
Marswalk is a web-based map tool that helps astronauts on the first human Mars mission plan surface excursions in Gale Crater and Mount Sharp. It currently displays an overhead map of Mars built from NASA Trek imagery, centered on the proposed landing site (137.4019° E, 4.5965° S). We have also built a pipeline that turns USGS elevation data into slope maps, and begun designing a route planner that compares a fastest route with a safest route between points of interest like Darwin Outcrop and The Kimberley.

The tool addresses the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge by turning NASA’s public data into something a crew can use to decide where to go and how to get there. This matters because astronauts will have no GPS and no roads, so good terrain information could be the difference between a productive excursion and a dangerous one. A map that connects scientific targets to safe paths helps crews explore more while staying safer.
details:
What it does and how it works:
Marswalk is a browser-based map of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, made for astronauts planning trips on the surface of Mars. Right now it shows a Mars map from NASA imagery, centered on the proposed landing site (137.4019° E, 4.5965° S). We also wrote a Python script that turns USGS elevation data into a slope map, and we planned a route finder that would show the fastest and a safest path between points of interest like Darwin Outcrop and The Kimberley. We ran out of time to get the points of interest and the routes working, so the submitted version only includes the map and landing site.

Benefits:
Once finished, the tool would give crews one view that connects interesting science targets to the terrain between them. Showing both a fast route and a safe route would let astronauts weigh the tradeoff themselves, using real NASA and USGS data.

Intended impact:
We want to show how NASA’s public data can help make the first human Mars mission safer and more efficient. The same approach could later be used for other landing sites and planets.

Tools, languages, and software

  • Mainly HTML and JavaScript, with some CSS
  • ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript
  • NASA Trek Viking Mars imagery and the MOLA elevation layer
  • USGS Mars Gale 1-meter elevation data
  • Python (NumPy, rasterio, Pillow)
  • VS Code and GitHub Codespaces
  • Google Docs for planning
  • AI assistance for brainstorming and coding (ChatGPT and Claude Sonnet 5.5)

We only needed laptops and a web browser. The elevation file is about 3.6 GB, so disk space mattered.

How it’s creative:
Instead of a plain map viewer, we aimed for a decision tool that compares a fast route with a safe route to real Curiosity locations, using slope calculated from actual Mars elevation data. We also included photos and took into consideration various important aspects astronauts could expect on their mission.

Factors we considered:

  • Data limits: the elevation data is sharper in some areas than others.
  • Safety: slope is only one hazard, so “safest” would only mean the gentlest terrain.
  • Scope and time: we prioritized a working map first, but getting a Mars map to display correctly took longer than expected, which left no time for routing.
  • Teamwork: we split up roles and kept our research in a shared document. Our biggest challenge stemmed from trying to include a part for each of our team members, while also trying to explain and align the project idea with each of their expectations in mind.
